Meanwhile, back at the ranch...

By: Johann Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The death bell may be tolling for the captive bred lion industry, but what will happen to the thousands of lions in captivity?

Summary:
The producers of Blood lions supplied us with extra footage of a lion hunt which took place in the kalahari on the botswana border. They also gave us an interview with the cameraman who filmed the hunt where he claims that especially three laws were broken on the hunt - 1) the lions were released only one day before the hunt started 2) the lions were drugged and 3) there was no nature conservation official present at the hunt
We will check his claims and then take the footage to nature conservation, the lion breeders association and phasa - ask them to watch the footage with the presenter and give us their comments on what they see. The cameraman also reported the hunt to the green scorpions, and therefore we will also take it to them and ask why nothing has been done. Since the Cook report government has been trying to root out canned hunting, but got themselves tied up in knots with technicalities, distinguishing between canned and captive bred. But now, overseas legislation seems to be achieving what we couldnt do ourselves Australia and France banned the import of lion trophies from SA. And then in Jan this year, the US banned the import of all lion trophies from Africa, unless you can prove that the specific hunt had a real benefit for the conservation of wild lions. 85% of captive bred lion hunters come from the US, and this may very well mean the end of the industry. At hte same time PHASA, our own professional hunters body, also turned their back on the captive bred industry - stating that they will expell any of their members who take part in such hunt. So what will happen to the 6 - 8 000 lions currently on lion breeding farms? Will the breeders further develop the trade in lion bones with China, or will they be able to prove to the IUCN that captive bred lions do hold a conservation value?

Expert:
Mr. Andrew Venter CEO Wildlands Conservation Trust
Mr. Stan Burger President Professional Hunters' Association of South Africa (PHASA)
Mr. Deon Swart Past Director of North West Conservation
Prof. Pieter Potgieter President South African Predator Association (SAPA)
Mr. Paul Stones Professional Hunter

Press Release:


Lion Hunting Industry
It’s been almost 20 years since the Cook Report exposed the cruelty associated with South Africa’s canned lion hunting industry. Despite these revelations, captive lion breeding has since developed into a billion rand industry. Now, following the recent US ban on the importation of lion trophies, the local industry is facing total collapse. This question remains: what does the future hold for up to 10 000 captive-bred lions on farms across the country? Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


Interviews:

The hunt:
Derek Gobbit Cameraman
Andre Venter Blood lions
Hans de Klerk? Ranch owner
Deon Swart? Ex NW Parks
Stan Phasa

New developments:
Andrew Venter Wildlands Trust
Prof Potgieter Lion breeders
Paul Stone Hunting outfitter
Stan Phasa

"Graphic:
Number of lion breeders = Unknown
Estimated = 400 (based on 2009 figures)

Number of lions in captivity = Unknown
Guestimate = 6000 – 10 000

Captive bred Lions hunted 2015:
Government figures: 540
SAPA figures: 750


State departments refusing on camerav interviews:
DEA
DAFF
Tourism" "Recent developments in the hunting industry have left lion breeders in dire straits. Breeders, hunters and the anti-hunting fraternity now have to face a question that’s lingered for 20 years – what are we going to do with the 1000's of lions in captivity when their owners can no longer afford to keep them?

Since January we've seen a massive 70 % decline in the number of lion hunts, and more and more breeders are desperately looking for a way out."

Derek: Link in the veld (preferable with lions) The captive bred lion hunting business has been shrouded in controversy since 1997, when the Cook report exposed the cruel and unethical way in which some of these hunts are conducted.
"These images of a lioness being shot next to a fence separating her from her cubs caused a global outcry. Overnight, the term “canned” hunting became part of the international vocabulary.

Government promised to close down the industry and committees and working groups were appointed to decide how to go about it. Long time professional hunter Paul Stones, is not convinced that the expose had any positive impact."

Paul: All it did was it tarred the industry with something that wasn't common practise. It tarred South Africa, as country, and, by and large at the end of it all, when it was all set and done, 20 years past, without any real change, and if anything, more and more captive bred lions were being hunted, but, we had the opportunity, this country had the opportunity to make sure that something like this never ever happened again, and we didn't.

V/o: In fact, today government seems to have lost almost all control over the industry. Their answers to us were vague, but it soon became clear that they don't know how many lions there are in captivity, or even how many registered lion breeders there are. Their figures are estimates based on older estimates and are castly different from those given to us by other sources. The original promise to close the industry took 10 years to make it to the law books.

And when the legislation was published in 2007, it looked set to close down the industry. It required that each lion be released for a period of 2 years before it could be hunted, making it impossible to hunt them in a profitable manner. The industry went to court, and won on a technicality, with the Supreme Court of Appeal ruling that the minister of environmental affairs had no jurisdiction on farmed animals.


Meanwhile, captive bred hunting had exploded into a billion rand industry, attracting mostly wealthy Americans wanting a guaranteed lion trophy in the shortest possible time. Almost 90% of these hunts happen in the North West province because they only require a 4 day release period, while other provinces require anything from a month onwards. Deon Swart, former director of nature conservation in North West, says it's all about the money.

Deon Swart: It is an economic driven principle. It's got nothing to do with conservation at all. These animals are bred to be hunted. And if you bring in more animals, or more clients, you can hunt more animals, it's very simple.
Cameraman Derek Gobbet, who films hunts for overseas clients, agrees.

Derek Gobbet: Sausage factory

A good example was the first captive bred lion hunt he filmed back in 2012. Local hunting outfitters Stormberg Elangeni, acted as facilitators for an American Outfitter who brought 10 clients to hunt 10 lions on De Klerk Safaris' farm Wilzenau in the Kalahari. The hunters shot 8 lions in the first 4 days, one on day 5 and number ten on day 9 as they were also hunting other animals on a different location during the same trip.

Derek says 4 lions were released the day before the clients arrived and another 4 on the day of their arrival, which would be illegal which is illegal, but land owner Hans de Klerk, who was not available for an on-camera interview, says that the releases Derek saw were meant for a future hunt, as he already released the 10 lions intended for their hunt the week before. He supplied transport permits for two groups of 10 lions and 2 “notification to hunt” documents as proof, but as the notifications have no official date stamp, critics could still question their validity.
However, North West Nature Conservation, who also refused an on-camera interview, said that the hunt was legal and all paperwork was in order. When we asked them to confirm if there was indeed a second 10 lion hunt straight after, they said that we would have to use the promotion of access to information act to get the information.
From the footage it is clear that no nature conservation official attended the hunt, – but North West Nature Conservation claims in their message that an official was present, and that “nothing irregular was reported”.

Footage of hunt

Even if the hunt was legal, it proves the sausage factory theory and then there are still question marks over how they were shot – de Klerk pointed out that those questions should be directed at Stormberg Elangeni, as he only supplied the lions and the land. But James Quin, from Stormberg Elangeni refused to speak to us, and simply sent a letter categorically denying that they did anything illegal.
These lions were raised in captivity and they’d had at most 4 days to adapt. The most disturbing hunts to watch are these of two lionesses shot out of trees, trying to hide from their pursuers, and this one cornered against a fence of sorts. It took half a dozen shots to kill this female, who’d crawled into a hole and, like the others, had nowhere to escape to."

Derek Gobbett: All just a lie


The SA predator association, SAPA was formed to try and clean up the industry and remove rogue elements. They have set strict rules for their members, but their problem is that membership is not mandatory. De Klerk Safaris is a current member of SAPA

Prof Pottie: Ek wil graag die versekering gee dat indien dit blyk dat daar dinge plaasgevind het wat of onwettig of oneties is, sal SAPA beslis onmiddellik ordentlik ondersoek daarna doen, en indien die feite dit regverdig sal daar beslis dissiplinere optrede kom.

Derek, possible link otherwise v/o But while the industry continued to grow, so did the associated controversy. In mid 2015, the powerful documentary Bloodlions hit the big screens around the world, condemning the captive bred lion industry.

Andrew Venter: The global conservation view is that what we're doing in this country around lions is wrong, and that our abuse of lions for commercial purposes and the associated fraud, deceit is just simply unethical.

And then, around same time, Zimbabwe's beloved Cecil the Lion, was hunted illegally by an American dentist from Minnesota. For weeks Cecil’s killing remained one of the most talked about topics on global social media. The dentist was forced to close his practise and go into hiding.
Following that, in November last year, at their AGM, our professional hunters association, PHASA broke their ties with the captive bred lion industry, banning any of their members from taking part in such hunts.

Stan Burger: It was obvious to Phasa that nothing was going to change at all as far as the captive bred industry goes, so that is why Phasa had no option but to distance ourselves from the captive bred industry.

And then, the likely death blow for the industry came in January this year - the US government banned the import of all lion trophies from Africa, unless it can be proven that the specific hunt makes a positive contribution to the conservation of lions in the wild.
Overnight hunts were cancelled, and Sapa knows they have to somehow comply if they are to survive
If you have to feed up to 1000 lions a day, as some breeders do, and if your income drops by 70%, you are in serious trouble

Prof Pottie: Dit maak ons seer

It doesn't help their case that two of our big NGO's are pushing a motion at IUCN later this year to condemn the industry.

Some breeders are already getting rid of their lions, offering cheap hunting packages to local hunters for the first time.
The Free State, where most breeders are, has seen a sharp increase in applications to euthanize “old lions” with about 20 applications since January to export their bones to the Far East for around R30 000 per lion. NW Nature Conservation, say they have already received 4 similar requests from lion breeders, including the biggest breeder in the country, stating the American legislation as the reason. So far, they haven't issued permits, but said they are investigating the merits of the request...."


PROMOS: We have 6,000 to 10,000 lions in captivity in South Africa, but this massive industry may be collapsing... what will the future hold for these kings behind bars?
In January the US banned the import of Lion hunting trophies with devastating effects on South Africa's lion breeding industry...

Prof Pottie: En dit dwing hulle nou om allerhand ander planne te maak.

Are these animals simply destined to be slaughtered for the Far East Lion Bone market?
Over the past 2 decades hunting captive bred lions in South Africa has been a booming business.

Deon Swart: It is an economic driven principle...

But has new American legislation banning the import of trophies finally dealt the lion breeding industry a death blow?
Other suggestions:

Almost 20 years since the Cook report first exposed canned lion hunting, have we managed to regulate the captive bred hunting industry?"
Captive-bred lion hunting: is new American legislation about to bring down a highly profitable industry?

The three relevant government departments, Environmental Affairs, Tourism and Agriculture declined on-camera interviews. In their written responses, all 3 were very vague about this issue. This will move to later in the story (WG)

The fact is that government does not even know how many lions there are in captivity, and our sources quote numbers, ranging between 6000 and 10000.

Government also does not know how many lion breeders there are - even though you need a permit to be registered as one.

Environmental Affairs says 540 captive bred lions were hunted last year. SAPA, the predator breeders association, pegs the number at closer to 750.

De Klerk Safaris is a current member of SAPA Prof Pottie: Ek wil graag die versekering gee dat indien dit blyk dat daar dinge plaasgevind het wat of onwettig of oneties is, sal SAPA beslis onmiddellik ordentlik ondersoek daarna doen, en indien die feite dit regverdig sal daar beslis dissiplinere optrede kom. Derek, possible link otherwise v/o But while the industry continued to grow, so did the associated controversy. In mid 2015, the powerful documentary Bloodlions hit the big screens around the world, condemning the captive bred lion industry. Andrew Venter: The global conservation view is that what we're doing in this country around lions is wrong, and that our abuse of lions for commercial purposes and the associated fraud, deceit is just simply unethical. And then, around same time, Zimbabwe's beloved Cecil the Lion, was hunted illegally by an American dentist from Minnesota. For weeks Cecil’s killing remained one of the most talked about topics on global social media. The dentist was forced to close his practise and go into hiding. Following that, in November last year, at their AGM, our professional hunters association, PHASA broke their ties with the captive bred lion industry, banning any of their members from taking part in such hunts. Stan Burger: It was obvious to Phasa that nothing was going to change at all as far as the captive bred industry goes, so that is why Phasa had no option but to distance ourselves from the captive bred industry. And then, the likely death blow for the industry came in January this year - the US government banned the import of all lion trophies from Africa, unless it can be proven that the specific hunt makes a positive contribution to the conservation of lions in the wild. Overnight hunts were cancelled, and Sapa knows they have to somehow comply if they are to survive If you have to feed up to 1000 lions a day, as some breeders do, and if your income drops by 70%, you are in serious trouble Prof Pottie: Dit maak ons seer It doesn't help their case that two of our big NGO's are pushing a motion at IUCN later this year to condemn the industry. Some breeders are already getting rid of their lions, offering cheap hunting packages to local hunters for the first time. The Free State, where most breeders are, has seen a sharp increase in applications to euthanize “old lions” with about 20 applications since January to export their bones to the Far East for around R30 000 per lion. NW Nature Conservation, say they have already received 4 similar requests from lion breeders, including the biggest breeder in the country, stating the American legislation as the reason. So far, they haven't issued permits, but said they are investigating the merits of the request...." PROMOS: We have 6,000 to 10,000 lions in captivity in South Africa, but this massive industry may be collapsing... what will the future hold for these kings behind bars? In January the US banned the import of Lion hunting trophies with devastating effects on South Africa's lion breeding industry... Prof Pottie: En dit dwing hulle nou om allerhand ander planne te maak. Are these animals simply destined to be slaughtered for the Far East Lion Bone market? Over the past 2 decades hunting captive bred lions in South Africa has been a booming business. Deon Swart: It is an economic driven principle... But has new American legislation banning the import of trophies finally dealt the lion breeding industry a death blow? Other suggestions: Almost 20 years since the Cook report first exposed canned lion hunting, have we managed to regulate the captive bred hunting industry?" Captive-bred lion hunting: is new American legislation about to bring down a highly profitable industry? The three relevant government departments, Environmental Affairs, Tourism and Agriculture declined on-camera interviews. In their written responses, all 3 were very vague about this issue. This will move to later in the story (WG) The fact is that government does not even know how many lions there are in captivity, and our sources quote numbers, ranging between 6000 and 10000. Government also does not know how many lion breeders there are - even though you need a permit to be registered as one. Environmental Affairs says 540 captive bred lions were hunted last year. SAPA, the predator breeders association, pegs the number at closer to 750.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The death bell may be tolling for the captive bred lion industry, but what will happen to the thousands of lions in captivity?
metadata.Summary: The producers of Blood lions supplied us with extra footage of a lion hunt which took place in the kalahari on the botswana border. They also gave us an interview with the cameraman who filmed the hunt where he claims that especially three laws were broken on the hunt - 1) the lions were released only one day before the hunt started 2) the lions were drugged and 3) there was no nature conservation official present at the hunt We will check his claims and then take the footage to nature conservation, the lion breeders association and phasa - ask them to watch the footage with the presenter and give us their comments on what they see. The cameraman also reported the hunt to the green scorpions, and therefore we will also take it to them and ask why nothing has been done. Since the Cook report government has been trying to root out canned hunting, but got themselves tied up in knots with technicalities, distinguishing between canned and captive bred. But now, overseas legislation seems to be achieving what we couldnt do ourselves Australia and France banned the import of lion trophies from SA. And then in Jan this year, the US banned the import of all lion trophies from Africa, unless you can prove that the specific hunt had a real benefit for the conservation of wild lions. 85% of captive bred lion hunters come from the US, and this may very well mean the end of the industry. At hte same time PHASA, our own professional hunters body, also turned their back on the captive bred industry - stating that they will expell any of their members who take part in such hunt. So what will happen to the 6 - 8 000 lions currently on lion breeding farms? Will the breeders further develop the trade in lion bones with China, or will they be able to prove to the IUCN that captive bred lions do hold a conservation value?
